paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Holloway took place in Greene County, North Carolina, in August 1903, when a posse searched for Holloway, a Black farm laborer accused of burglary and an attempted assault on a white woman, and the sheriff hid him and took him to Goldsboro to keep him from being lynched. Holloway was convicted at Snow Hill in September and sentenced to hang, and in October he was again moved out of the county to avoid a lynching. Governor Charles B. Aycock commuted the sentence to life imprisonment in December because the identification rested entirely on the woman's recognition of his voice.

According to a Goldsboro dispatch of September 12, Holloway was curing tobacco with his employer, Tuton, when he was sent to the house for tools. The dispatch said that he slipped inside during a rain, hid under a bed, came out as Mrs. Tuton passed, made "improper proposals" and caught hold of her, and ran away when she screamed.

Mrs. Tuton told her husband, who "organized a posse and went in search of the negro." The sheriff reached Holloway first, "near day" in the News and Observer's text and "next day" in the Wilmington Messenger's, then hid him and brought him to Goldsboro "to keep him from being lynched." No report describes a meeting between the posse and the sheriff or any injury to Holloway.

He stayed in the Goldsboro jail until court week at Snow Hill. He was convicted in Greene County Superior Court before Judge Fred Moore and on September 12 was sentenced to be hanged on October 16; there was no appeal.

Holloway's counsel then asked for time to show that the woman had been mistaken in identifying him by his voice. Former judge W. S. O'B. Robinson told the governor that a man who had slept with Holloway that night had since gone insane and cried out in his ravings that Holloway was not the man. With the support of the trial judge and the prosecuting solicitor, Aycock respited Holloway to December 17. Before the respite was made public, Holloway was moved to the Wayne County jail, which the Richmond Times-Dispatch said was done "to avoid the possibility of a lynching," as feeling was strong against him around Snow Hill.

After a second respite, Aycock commuted the sentence on December 21 to life imprisonment at hard labor. His published reasons quoted Judge Moore, who had discussed the case with eight jurors and recommended commutation while still believing Holloway guilty. The governor added that six jurors had signed a written request and that there was "too much uncertainty to justify the taking of human life."

All of the coverage found came from white newspapers; no report in the Black press was found. The Goldsboro dispatch ran almost word for word in the Raleigh News and Observer and the Richmond Times-Dispatch on September 13 and in the Wilmington Semi-Weekly Messenger and the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic on September 15. Those texts said that "the negro" had "committed burglary and attempted an assault" upon "a most estimable white lady," stating the accusation as fact, and the Times-Dispatch headed its version "Negro Will Hang for Heinous Crime." The posse and the sheriff's move to prevent a lynching took up a single sentence and drew no comment.

Farther away, the Washington Evening Star gave the conviction a short paragraph, and the Spokane Press ran the respite as "Negro's Mad Ravings Saved Another Man." A Times-Dispatch news digest on the day of the respite called Holloway "the negro murderer," a charge that appears in no report of the case. By December the emphasis had shifted: the News and Observer's "His Neck Saved," reprinted by the Goldsboro Weekly Argus, printed the governor's reasons in full under the subhead "Convicted Because of His Voice."

The September reports named the woman Mrs. Tuton and placed the crime in the afternoon, while later Raleigh reports called her "Mrs. Nelson" or "Mrs. Hulon" and placed the entry at night; the News and Observer and the Times-Dispatch also gave different respite dates. The Spokane item said the governor himself ordered the October removal; the Raleigh dispatch named no one.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Holloway
bases: A posse organized by the accuser's husband searched for Holloway, and the sheriff hid him and moved him to Goldsboro 'to keep him from being lynched' (A1, A3); he was again moved out of Greene county in October to avoid a lynching (A6, A9); no violence against him is reported, so this is a threatened, not an attempted or completed, lynching.

The posse and the first removal rest on one Goldsboro dispatch (A1, A3), but the danger of lynching is reported again, independently, in October Raleigh dispatches (A6, A9), and the conviction, respite and commutation are reported by several separate correspondents (A1, A5, A6, A11, A12, A14).

accounts.label: Goldsboro correspondent (September)
accounts.gist: Holloway hid in the Tuton house during a rain while sent for tools, made improper proposals and grabbed Mrs. Tuton, then fled; the husband's posse searched for him, and the sheriff found and hid him to prevent a lynching.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondents (October-December)
accounts.gist: Holloway was convicted of entering a woman's house at night on her recognition of his voice; a man who slept with him that night, now insane, says Holloway is not the man, and the governor found too much doubt to hang him.

accounts.label: Governor Aycock's statement
accounts.gist: Identification depended entirely on recognition of the voice; the trial judge, six to eight jurors and many leading citizens asked for commutation.

framing.detail: September headlines 'Holloway to Hang' and 'Negro Will Hang for Heinous Crime' stated the accusation as fact and called the accuser 'a most estimable white lady', mentioning the posse and the lynching danger without comment.
October and December Raleigh dispatches and the News & Observer's 'His Neck Saved' reported the doubts over voice identification and printed the governor's reasons in full.
Distant papers ran short wire items, the Spokane Press under 'Negro's Mad Ravings Saved Another Man'.

Sentence commuted to life imprisonment at hard labor on Dec. 21, 1903, on Judge Moore's recommendation after he consulted eight jurors; the governor found 'too much uncertainty' to take a life.
